name: Acute Gastroenteritis

pathogens.why: Watery non-inflammatory diarrhea is predominantly viral or toxin-mediated; invasive bacterial pathogens are more strongly associated with bloody stool, high fever, and systemic symptoms (see Dysentery).

investigations.test: None routinely required in mild self-limited cases
investigations.why: Most cases resolve without specific identification of organism.

investigations.test: Stool routine/microscopy (if symptoms persist beyond 7 days or in immunocompromised)
investigations.why: Identifies parasitic causes (e.g., Giardia) that require specific therapy.

reason: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea without high fever or systemic toxicity is most consistent with viral or toxin-mediated gastroenteritis. Antibiotics do not shorten illness duration in this setting and may prolong carriage of certain pathogens. Oral rehydration is the priority intervention.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Ch 49 (Diarrhea and Constipation, p.302-307); Ch 138 (Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning, p.1076-1082); Ch 209 (Viral Gastroenteritis, p.1627-1630)
clinicalPearls: More than 90% of acute diarrhea episodes are infectious, and most are mild and self-limited; vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain frequently accompany the illness (p.305).

The first decision point is to separate noninflammatory (watery, small-bowel, enterotoxin/viral) from inflammatory (dysenteric, colonic, invasion/cytotoxin) disease, since this dichotomy drives the need for stool studies and therapy (p.1078-1079).

Clinical timing offers etiologic clues: an abrupt illness with prominent vomiting and little or no fever within hours of eating points to a preformed toxin (e.g., S. aureus, B. cereus), whereas high fever with significant abdominal pain points to invasive or cytotoxin-producing organisms (p.305).
Vomiting can be the predominant or sole presenting feature of viral gastroenteritis, especially in children (p.1629).
Bloody diarrhea with only low-grade fever or no fever should specifically raise concern for Shiga toxin-producing/enterohemorrhagic E. coli (p.1079, p.1081).
Bulky pale/grey stools suggest a malabsorptive small-bowel process, while profuse 'rice-water' stools suggest cholera or a similar toxigenic secretory process (p.1078).

Reduced gastric acidity (achlorhydria, gastric surgery, or acid-suppressing drugs such as PPIs/H2 blockers) lowers the infectious barrier and increases susceptibility to Salmonella, Giardia, and other enteric pathogens (p.1077).

Immunocompromised hosts (cell-mediated defects/AIDS, hypogammaglobulinemia) get more severe, protracted, and sometimes invasive disease, and may harbor opportunistic pathogens not seen in immunocompetent patients (p.1080, p.305).
Tenesmus and frequent small-volume stools indicate a distal colonic/proctitis process (e.g., shigellosis, amebiasis) rather than a small-bowel secretory process (p.1078).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute infectious diarrhea results when an ingested pathogen overwhelms or bypasses host defenses (gastric acid, intestinal motility/peristalsis, mucus layer, secretory IgA, and the protective resident microbiota). Mechanistically there are two broad patterns. Noninflammatory disease arises in the proximal small bowel and is mediated by enterotoxins (e.g., cholera toxin, E. coli heat-labile [LT] and heat-stable [ST] toxins) or by viral injury; cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a GTP-binding protein to persistently activate adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, increasing chloride secretion and decreasing sodium absorption, producing watery secretory diarrhea without mucosal destruction. Inflammatory disease affects the colon or distal small bowel through mucosal invasion (Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Salmonella) or cytotoxins (S. dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, C. difficile), destroying epithelium and producing dysentery with fecal leukocytes. Viral pathogens (norovirus, rotavirus) injure the small-intestinal villous epithelium: rotavirus destroys mature absorptive enterocytes and the loss of brush-border enzymes leaves unmetabolized disaccharides, generating combined secretory and osmotic diarrhea, with the nonstructural protein NSP4 acting as an enterotoxin. Crucially, glucose-coupled sodium absorption in the small intestine remains intact even during toxin-driven secretion, which is the physiologic basis for oral rehydration therapy (p.1076-1077, p.1081, p.1629).
additionalDifferentials: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7 / Shiga toxin-producing) - watery progressing to bloody, HUS risk
Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) - profuse rice-water secretory diarrhea
Preformed-toxin food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens)
Sapovirus, astrovirus, enteric adenovirus types 40/41 (viral, mainly young children)
Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia (esp. travelers, hikers, immunocompromised, persistent cases)
infectionMimics: Enteric fever / typhoid (penetrating pathogens Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica with fever, relative bradycardia, splenomegaly)
Yersinia enterocolitica terminal ileitis mimicking acute appendicitis
Clostridioides difficile colitis (recent or current antibiotics; predominant nosocomial cause)
Acute viral hepatitis A and other systemic infections (legionellosis, listeriosis, toxic shock, malaria) in which diarrhea is one feature
SARS-CoV-2 - diarrhea can be an early symptom
nonInfectiousMimics: Medication side effects (antibiotics, NSAIDs, antidysrhythmics, antihypertensives, some antidepressants, chemotherapy, laxatives) - the most common noninfectious cause
Ischemic colitis (age >50, lower abdominal pain preceding watery then bloody diarrhea, spares rectum)
Colonic diverticulitis; partial bowel obstruction; graft-versus-host disease
Initial presentation or flare of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis) with abrupt onset mimicking infection
Toxic ingestions (organophosphates, amanita/other mushrooms, arsenic) and seafood toxins (ciguatera, scombroid)
Food allergy including alpha-gal (delayed mammalian-meat allergy) which can cause systemic collapse and be mistaken for dehydration
additionalInvestigations: Fecal leukocyte smear (methylene blue) or, more sensitively, fecal lactoferrin to distinguish inflammatory from noninflammatory disease
Culture-independent multiplex nucleic-acid amplification (PCR) stool panels - now first-line for severe/domestically acquired disease; faster and more sensitive than culture
Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter in febrile inflammatory diarrhea acquired outside hospital
Sorbitol-MacConkey plating / Shiga-toxin or PCR testing when EHEC (E. coli O157:H7) is suspected (visibly bloody stool)
Specific antigen/microscopy for Giardia and Cryptosporidium, and antigen detection for E. histolytica, when suspected or in persistent diarrhea
Examination for ova and parasites if diarrhea persists beyond ~10 days
Nosocomial diarrhea workup should focus on C. difficile toxin testing; routine stool culture in the hospital is low-yield
Endoscopy/imaging reserved for persistent (>30 day) or suspected noninfectious disease; not indicated during the acute episode (risk of false-positive results)
redFlags: Signs of severe dehydration: lethargy/obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, shock
Diarrhea persisting >48 h without improvement (or >2 weeks suggesting a different chronic spectrum)
Severe abdominal pain in a patient aged >50 years
Bloody diarrhea with low-grade or absent fever (EHEC / HUS warning)
harrison.prognosis: Most acute infectious gastroenteritis is self-limited and resolves within days; viral norovirus/sapovirus illness typically lasts 1-3 days and rotavirus 3-7 days. Death is uncommon in healthy adults but occurs chiefly from dehydration in infants and debilitated elderly; globally acute diarrhea remains a leading cause of childhood death. Oral rehydration has dramatically reduced mortality (e.g., cholera case fatality from >50% untreated to <1%). Recognized post-infectious sequelae include reactive arthritis (after invasive Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter/Yersinia), Guillain-Barre syndrome (after Campylobacter), hemolytic-uremic syndrome (after Shiga toxin-producing bacteria), post-infectious IBS (notably after Campylobacter), and transient post-infectious lactase deficiency; recurrent childhood diarrhea in resource-poor settings causes environmental enteropathy with growth and developmental stunting (p.302, p.305, p.1077-1078, p.1081, p.1628-1629).
pitfalls: Avoid antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide) and bismuth-based slowing in febrile or bloody/dysenteric diarrhea - they may prolong fever and pathogen shedding in Shigella and other invasive infections; in viral gastroenteritis antibiotics and antimotility agents are not indicated.

Do NOT give antibiotics when enterohemorrhagic (Shiga toxin-producing) E. coli is suspected, because antibiotics can increase toxin production and markedly raise the risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome.
Opioid/antimotility therapy can increase the frequency of bacteremia in Salmonella gastroenteritis and prolonged illness in Shigella.
Most acute diarrhea needs no microbiologic workup; routine extensive stool testing of mild self-limited disease wastes resources.
Do not screen for or endoscope to exclude celiac/Crohn disease or IBD during an acute episode - the risk is low and false-positive results are common.

A positive multiplex PCR panel may detect multiple organisms or carriage and can be hard to interpret; lack of an isolate prevents susceptibility testing and outbreak typing, so culture confirmation is still advised after a positive bacterial PCR.
Empirical antibacterial coverage is warranted regardless of pathogen recovery in selected high-risk patients (immunocompromised, prosthetic/mechanical heart valves, recent vascular grafts, elderly).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is graded clinically by functional impact and dehydration rather than by a single score. Mild: activity unrestricted. Moderate: activities altered. Severe: incapacitated. Dehydration assessment is the key severity measure on examination - mild = thirst, dry mouth, reduced axillary sweat, decreased urine output, slight weight loss; moderate = orthostatic blood-pressure fall, skin tenting, sunken eyes (or sunken fontanelle in infants); severe = lethargy/obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock. Frequency of stools forewarns impending dehydration. By duration, diarrhea is acute (<2 weeks), persistent (2-4 weeks), or chronic (>4 weeks) (p.302/304, p.307, p.1078).
